title: A Little-Known Secret To Effective Teaching
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes a rarely discussed strategy: the instant a teacher notices students doing exactly what was asked, the teacher should go silent and physically withdraw, allowing students to experience success entirely on their own. He explains the technique step by step—easing back without sudden movement, observing from a distance, and staying silent until the task concludes—while cautioning that it only works if the teacher has already taught and checked for understanding beforehand. The rationale is that unassisted success builds deep self-confidence and lets students enter a 'flow state' where the fastest growth and improvement occur. He acknowledges this runs counter to the conditioning most teachers have received to always appear busy and 'teaching,' and that biting one's tongue is difficult for habitual narrators and interrupters. The article frames restraint, not more instruction, as the transformative move once expectations are clear.
points: The core strategy: the moment students begin doing exactly what was asked, the teacher should go quiet and physically withdraw from the situation.
The technique requires clear prior instruction and a thorough check for understanding before students are sent off to work.
Unassisted success is said to build deep self-confidence and give students room to enter a highly productive 'flow state.'
The approach runs counter to the common belief that good teaching must always look active and busy.
Teachers who habitually narrate, interrupt, and add their own commentary will find the discipline to stay silent especially difficult but essential.
quotes: The split second you recognize your students doing what you want or asked of them, you clam up and allow them to experience success all on their own.

Using no sudden movements, slowly ease back and away from your class. Once you reach a distance from which you can observe every student, stay silent and in one place until the task is either finished or no longer successful.
You must never send your students off on their own unless they’ve proven to you that they know what is expected.
The reason the strategy is so effective is that whenever students experience success without interference, they gain deep confidence in themselves and their own abilities.
We’ve become conditioned to always be “teaching.” We’ve been brainwashed by the powers that be into believing that good teaching looks busy.
But to make this potentially game-changing strategy work, you must purge yourself from this falsehood.
